clue.text: Counsel of jocular nature may cause

definitions.text: Counsel of jocular nature may cause

parts.words: Counsel of jocular nature may cause
parts.note: a barrister making a joke during a trial sets off the merriment that court reporters record in brackets

explanation.surface: A remark on what a witty barrister can provoke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counsel' is a barrister, not advice; the reaction is the one law reports note when the room chuckles at a quip.
explanation.definitionFit: Court reports note the merriment provoked when a barrister or judge cracks a joke during proceedings.

clue.text: Big shot at a party? She's a big how!

clue.text: It's so extreme to talk more than anyone.

parts.note: to utter is to speak or say aloud
doing something the most means doing it more than anyone else

explanation.surface: A complaint that the person who talks most is going too far.
explanation.definitionFit: Uttermost means farthest or greatest in degree, the outermost limit.

clue.text: To be thus handed is very awkward.

definitions.text: To be thus handed is very awkward.

parts.words: To be thus handed is very awkward.
parts.note: the clue asks which word goes before 'handed' to make a compound meaning clumsy or tactless

explanation.surface: An observation that being handed something in a particular way is uncomfortable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handed' looks like passing an object; it completes a compound adjective for clumsiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone heavy-handed acts clumsily or without tact, so the word completes that compound.

clue.text: "With Fate conspire To grasp this Scheme of Things ——"

definitions.text: "With Fate conspire To grasp this Scheme of Things ——"

parts.words: "With Fate conspire To grasp this Scheme of Things ——"
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, whose missing final word rhymes with 'conspire'

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian verse with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The quatrain runs 'Ah Love! could you and I with Fate conspire / To grasp this sorry Scheme of Things entire'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's line ends on this word, meaning whole or complete, rhyming with 'conspire'.

clue.text: Had a collision, so, it seems, the child pretended.

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
acted means played a part, pretended

explanation.surface: A child crashed, or so it appeared, while playing make-believe.
explanation.definitionFit: Impacted means struck forcefully against something, a synonym for colliding.

clue.text: Yes, it needs real heroes to give chips !

definitions.text: Yes, it needs real heroes to give chips !

parts.words: Yes, it needs real heroes to give chips !
parts.note: the heroes are winners, but the same name was borne by a once-popular potato variety, the kind that gives chips

explanation.surface: A jokey claim that only genuine heroes can provide fried potatoes.
explanation.walkthrough: Champion was a widely grown nineteenth-century potato variety, so the winners' title doubles as a source of chips.
explanation.definitionFit: Winners of contests are given this title, and it was also an old potato variety used for frying.

clue.text: Carry out a bit of joinery work.

definitions.text: Carry out a bit of joinery work.

parts.words: Carry out a bit of joinery work.
parts.note: joinery suggests carpentry, but doing some joining simply means bringing things together

explanation.surface: An instruction to do some carpentry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joinery' suggests a woodworker's trade; the verb wanted just means to join.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring together or combine is the plain sense of joining, which joinery work does.

clue.text: Having had several more than one over the eight?

definitions.text: Having had several more than one over the eight?

parts.words: Having had several more than one over the eight?
parts.note: 'one over the eight' is British slang for one drink too many, so several more leaves someone even drunker

explanation.surface: A question about someone who has drunk far beyond their limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for slightly drunk; 'tight' is slang for drunk, so having had more makes the comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is slang for drunk, and the comparative describes someone more intoxicated still.

clue.text: Ex-member of society.

parts.note: not a former club member but someone rejected and expelled from the community

explanation.surface: A description of someone who has left a club or association.
explanation.definitionFit: A pariah rejected by society is no longer a member of it.

clue.text: Sportive procedure.

parts.note: the playful, sporting way of carrying on, as opposed to working

explanation.surface: A phrase describing how a game is run.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking part in a game or frolicking is the sportive activity described.

clue.text: How Tennyson's Queen o' the May to be called.

definitions.text: How Tennyson's Queen o' the May to be called.

parts.words: How Tennyson's Queen o' the May to be called.
parts.note: in Tennyson's poem The May Queen the girl asks her mother to wake and call her at a particular time

explanation.surface: A question about what title Tennyson's May Queen was given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Called' suggests a name, but the poem's refrain is 'You must wake and call me early, call me early, mother dear'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's refrain asks to be called at the start of the morning, before the usual hour.

clue.text: Not normally one who takes in stolen

definitions.text: Not normally one who takes in stolen

parts.words: Not normally one who takes in stolen
parts.note: someone who takes things in is a receiver, but ordinarily not a receiver of stolen goods

explanation.surface: A remark that this person is not usually a fence.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'receiver' is slang for a fence; the answer receives things but normally innocently.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who receives something is one who takes it in, normally lawfully.

clue.text: Goa bit too far when toasting!

definitions.text: Goa bit too far when toasting

parts.words: Goa bit too far when toasting
parts.note: toasting suggests raising glasses, but overdoing the toasting of bread burns its surface

explanation.surface: A warning against overdoing the speeches at a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toasting' looks like drinking healths; it is browning bread, and going too far burns it.
explanation.definitionFit: Overdoing heat on bread burns it slightly on the surface.

clue.text: In which the row works up to a climax.

definitions.text: In which the row works up to a climax.

parts.words: In which the row works up to a climax.
parts.note: row reads as a quarrel but means noise, which in music grows steadily louder

explanation.surface: A description of an argument escalating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel; here it is noise, swelling in volume in a musical passage.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, a gradual increase in loudness builds towards a peak.

clue.text: One braid that's enough for an elegant out.

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of the two words are put out of their order

explanation.surface: A single plait is all it takes for a stylish outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges ONE BRAID into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Debonair describes someone suave, stylish and confident in manner.

clue.text: Possible ration of a new local.

indicators.note: possible tells us one possible rearrangement of the words that follow is wanted

explanation.surface: A thought about what portion a new pub might serve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possible' rearranges A NEW LOCAL; a 'local' is British for a neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A ration is a fixed amount allotted, which is what an allowance is.

clue.text: Cast disparagement here — till beet emerges!

indicators.note: emerges suggests a new form arising from the jumbled letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a vegetable plot until the beetroot comes up.
explanation.definitionFit: To disparage someone is to make them seem small or unimportant.

clue.text: They really are the limit, each of them!

definitions.text: They really are the limit, each of them!

parts.words: They really are the limit, each of them!
parts.note: 'the limit' sounds like exasperation at people, but each outer bound literally is a limit

explanation.surface: An exasperated complaint about a group of troublesome people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They really are the limit' sounds like a grumble; taken literally each item is an outermost point.
explanation.definitionFit: The outermost points of a range are its furthest limits.

clue.text: The poor man's one possession.

parts.note: in Nathan's parable in the Second Book of Samuel the poor man owned nothing but a single young female sheep

explanation.surface: A remark about the only thing a needy man owns.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2 Samuel 12 the prophet Nathan tells David of a rich man who took the poor man's only animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathan's parable describes the poor man's sole treasure, a young female sheep, now a phrase for one's dearest possession.

clue.text: Fit out once more, that's some compensation.

definitions.meaning: to clothe or equip again, read as a re- prefix on the verb
amends or reparation for a wrong

explanation.surface: Being re-clothed counts as some recompense.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing again is re-dressing, and amends for a wrong is redress.

clue.text: Working well, that's obvious.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads 'Working well, that's obvious.': 'Working well' defines it but 'that's obvious' supplies no second sense or wordplay; probably garbled in the OCR.

clue.text: Shows aptitude, yes, but frail somehow.

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the word frail are arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: Someone has talent, admittedly, though they seem a bit weak.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural talent or knack is an aptitude.

clue.text: Pulled along up the aisle 7

definitions.meaning: hauled behind a vehicle with a rope
walking up the aisle means going to marry, split into two words

explanation.surface: Someone is dragged up the aisle to their wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Hauled by a rope is the first sense; split as two words it means going to marry.

clue.text: A gigantic chap must get browned off about it.

indicators.note: about means the browned word goes round the other one

parts.note: tanned skin is browned by the sun, so tan
taken as written

explanation.surface: A big man is bound to be fed up about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browned off' reads as British slang for fed up, a misleading phrase; 'off' is only a link word here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were giants of Greek myth, so the name is used for any giant.

clue.text: Fancy, opposing making a profit on stone !

parts.note: a gain is a profit
st is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at someone against making money on stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' is an exclamation, not part of the wordplay. ST is the abbreviation of the stone, a British weight of 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Being opposed to something means being in opposition to it.

clue.text: Strained this, in indication of time.

parts.note: taken as written
a verb's tense indicates the time of the action, past, present or future

explanation.surface: Someone felt stressed about this time signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indication of time' points to grammar: a verb's tense tells when something happens.
explanation.definitionFit: A strained atmosphere is one of extreme or highly charged feeling.
